proposals.name: Form matches and amplifies content
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's structural form (verse, an unbroken dialogue-only scene, fragmented interior monologue, essay-like exposition, etc.) is a deliberate choice that does communicative work, versus defaulting to conventional linear prose-scene structure regardless of content. High: the form itself carries meaning -- e.g., a poem whose rhyme/meter lands the story's turn, or a piece built entirely from one dialogue exchange that reveals character through the exchange alone. Low: the story could be re-typeset as ordinary paragraph narration and lose nothing; the form is generic and unconsidered.
proposals.rationale: Explains why the dense model rates R01 (told entirely as rhyming verse) and R04 (told entirely as one unbroken Socratic classroom dialogue) very highly (dense_pct .967 and .945) while the scorecard rates both near the bottom (card_pct .083 and .081) -- a checklist of generic prose-craft items (setting, description, pacing) has no natural slot for 'form itself as content.' R28's fragmented, clipped-sentence prose-poem style (dense_pct .986, card_pct .130) shows the same pattern.

proposals.name: Earned tonal whiplash after real buildup
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story builds genuine tension, grandeur, or dread and then deliberately punctures or juxtaposes it for effect, versus simply telling one flat joke with nothing built up to undercut. High: a mock-epic or horrific moment is followed by a sudden bathetic deflation, or a violent scene is framed by incongruous cozy/domestic detail, recontextualizing what came before. Low: the story is a single-beat gag -- its entire content is the punchline, with no contrasting register established first.
proposals.rationale: R01 builds mock-epic 'first steps on an alien world' imagery across a dozen lines, then deflates it with 'Dave handed Tom 10 quid'; R35 frames an on-page murder inside a cozy narrator-nibbling-a-cookie domestic scene at start and end. Both score dense_high/card_low (.967/.083 and .924/.142). By contrast R07, a pure two-sentence single-beat gag, scores card_high/dense_low (.997/.182) -- a scorecard rewarding 'humor present' can't distinguish earned whiplash from a flat pun.

proposals.name: Unifying refrain or extended metaphor structures the piece
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story uses a repeated phrase, image, or sustained metaphor that structures the piece and deepens in meaning on each repetition, versus using repetition only as filler or using no unifying device at all. High: a refrain opens and closes the piece, and its meaning has shifted by the final occurrence because of what happened between. Low: no structuring device is present, or a repeated phrase never accrues new meaning.
proposals.rationale: R33 bookends with 'To serve is the highest honour,' which lands very differently at the end (after a death) than at the start; R14 repeats 'I was too late to stop it' across three escalating instances that reframe the narrator's guilt each time. Both are dense_high/card_low (.966/.183 and .861/.049), suggesting the dense model rewards a structural device a discrete-item bank has no natural slot for.

proposals.name: Ending resists tidy, fully-explained closure
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the ending earns ambiguity, restraint, or an unresolved note appropriate to the material, versus wrapping every open thread into one explanatory line that fully resolves the story. High: the last line raises a question, leaves a moral stance open, or trusts the reader to sit with something unresolved. Low: the ending exists purely to deliver a reveal or pun that snaps the whole piece shut with full explanation.
proposals.rationale: R04 ends the entire piece on a student's unanswered question, deferred to a future lecture; R17 ends on the flatly unresolved 'I'm done comparing.' Both dense_high/card_low (.945/.081 and .935/.062). Contrast with card_high pieces like R34 and R30 (.965/.158-range card scores), which close by having a character fully explain or neatly resolve the joke/threat in the last exchange.

proposals.name: Story stands alone without external paratext
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story is complete and comprehensible using only the text given, versus depending on embedded links to the author's other posts, references to an ongoing personal saga/continuity, or footer plugs to feel complete or land its appeal. High: no fact needed to understand the story is missing from the text itself. Low: the piece leans on 'this is part of an ongoing saga,' hyperlinked backstory, or a subreddit plug to feel finished.
proposals.rationale: R02 is explicitly 'story #1385 in a row' in an 'ongoing saga,' with several embedded hyperlinks substituting for on-page worldbuilding; R08 is marked 'a continuation of a series of earlier prompt responses' with a linked precursor needed for full context. Both score card_high/dense_low (.850/.027 and .865/.093) -- the scorecard does not appear to discount reliance on paratext the way the dense reader, who can't see the linked material, does.

proposals.name: Contains actual invented narrative content, not meta-text
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the submission contains narrative content -- a scene, character, or event responding to the prompt -- versus being non-fiction/meta-text such as an automated moderator notice, or having its actual story diluted by a large proportion of framing text (serialization notices, self-promotion, links) rather than invented content. High: the text is substantially a scene or character doing something. Low: little or none of the text is fictional content; it is administrative, procedural, or self-promotional framing.
proposals.rationale: R11 is literally an automated subreddit-moderator removal notice ('Your post has been removed as it is not tagged correctly... This is an automated message') with zero narrative content, yet scores card_pct=.885 while dense_pct=.007 correctly identifies it as not a story at all -- the clearest scorecard failure in the slice. R02 shows an attenuated version of the same issue: a real story is trailed by a lengthy self-promotional/continuity footer ('story #1385 in a row... collected at this link'), and it too is card_high/dense_low (.850/.027).

proposals.name: Backstory dramatized in scene, not narrated in dialogue
proposals.instruction: Judge whether necessary backstory or world-mechanics are revealed through scene, action, or sensory detail the reader witnesses directly, versus delivered as a character's spoken explanation or narrator info-dump ('as-you-know' exposition). High: we learn the rules or history by watching them operate. Low: a character stops to explain, in dialogue or monologue, how the world, power, or threat works.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R39 both resolve their central mystery by having a character explicitly explain the mechanism aloud ('I took over your friend, and you thought you defeated me!'; a dialogue recap of 'the Ensemble' and the 'Treaty of Silence'). Both are card_high/dense_low (.897/.054 and .994/.148). Contrast with R26, which dramatizes an entire dragon-bonding ritual through physical action with no explanatory narration at all, and is dense_high/card_low (.947/.093).

proposals.name: Distinct, consistent narrative voice or idiolect
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the prose has a specific, consistent diction, rhythm, and sensibility that feels like it belongs to this narrator and no other, versus generic, interchangeable competent prose. High: a random sentence pulled out of context is identifiable as belonging to this piece. Low: the sentences are serviceable but could be dropped into many other genre stories unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R27's narrator sustains an ironic, baroque essayistic register throughout ('baroque in execution,' jokes about 'the decorative swan'); R19's serial-killer narrator holds a flat, matter-of-fact confessional cadence that never breaks even describing murder. Both dense_high/card_low (.924/.073 and .939/.155) -- a strong idiosyncratic voice is exactly the kind of holistic property that resists decomposition into discrete scorecard items.

proposals.name: Story premise follows its own internal rules
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's fantastical mechanism (magic, power, technology) operates by rules that are established and then honored, versus being hand-waved or invoked ad hoc whenever convenient. High: the mechanism's logic is worked through and events follow from it, even if the premise itself is a joke. Low: a character explicitly shrugs off explaining how their power/magic works, or the mechanism's rules visibly change to fit whatever the scene needs.
proposals.rationale: R04 is built entirely as a rigorous, escalating logical argument about the Schrodinger's-cat thought experiment, extending real reasoning step by step (dense_high/card_low .945/.081). Contrast with R31, card_high/dense_low (.914/.140), where the resurrection power is explicitly left unexplained ('I don't know. It just happens when I want to do it'), and R16, also card_high/dense_low (.965/.158), where creation's entire logic is 'I was on a budget,' with no rule beyond the joke.

proposals.name: Reframes the prompt instead of executing it literally
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story takes the prompt's premise somewhere the prompt didn't already state -- a genuine reinterpretation, inversion, or new angle -- versus fulfilling the most obvious, literal reading of the prompt with stock genre furniture. High: after reading the story, the prompt itself reads differently or more richly. Low: the story simply re-enacts what the prompt already told you would happen.
proposals.rationale: R33 takes a prompt about a dying 'Immortal' master and reveals only gradually that the narrator is a devoted animal and the 'Immortals' are simply long-lived humans, recontextualizing the whole premise; R17 turns a wish-fulfillment 'you have more heaven-points than your grandma' prompt into a meditation on self-serving virtue rather than a power fantasy. Both dense_high/card_low (.966/.183 and .935/.062). Contrast with R13, card_high/dense_low (.942/.147), which executes 'put a Coen Brothers character into your favorite show' completely literally with no reframing beyond the crossover mechanics.

proposals.name: Attempts a genuinely difficult narrative task
proposals.instruction: Judge how technically or imaginatively difficult the thing the story attempts is, independent of full success -- e.g., rendering a non-human or incomprehensible consciousness legible, compressing an institution's history into one piece, sustaining a rigorous argument -- versus attempting the easiest available version of the prompt. High: the writer visibly took on a hard problem. Low: the writer resolved the prompt in the least effortful way that technically satisfies it.
proposals.rationale: R03 attempts to render the interior emotional experience of a literally 'barely comprehensible' eldritch being and make it read as a genuine love story (dense_high/card_low .998/.192); R27 compresses an entire fictional social institution's centuries of history into one satirical piece. Contrast with R07, card_high/dense_low (.997/.182), which resolves 'a writer falls in love with a character' in two sentences via the most minimal possible reading.

proposals.name: Fresh, precise figurative language at sentence level
proposals.instruction: Judge whether individual sentences contain original, precise imagery or figuration, versus flat, functional, or clichéd phrasing (stock adjectives, dead metaphors, 'evil grin'-style shorthand). High: several images or turns of phrase could not have been produced by swapping synonyms into a generic sentence. Low: description leans on stock phrases, and the prose could be summarized without losing any texture.
proposals.rationale: R03 produces original images like 'great wafting waves of energy' and 'the math that made me into existence'; R27 turns abstraction into fresh comic imagery ('eating the decorative swan at a banquet before it has had time to preen itself'). Both dense_high/card_low (.998/.192 and .924/.073). Contrast with the more functional, plot-transactional prose of card_high pieces like R39 (card_pct .994) and R18 (card_pct .847).

proposals.name: Dialogue reveals character, not just plot info
proposals.instruction: Judge whether dialogue exchanges do double duty -- advancing the plot while also revealing personality, values, or psychology the reader wouldn't otherwise learn -- versus dialogue that exists only to transact information the plot needs. High: delete the plot information being conveyed and the exchange would still tell you something true about who these people are. Low: strip the information being conveyed and nothing about character remains.
proposals.rationale: R04's Socratic dialogue reveals a student's escalating intelligence and a professor's genuine respect purely through the shape of the questions (dense_high/card_low .945/.081); R06's rambling improvised villain monologue reveals an entire comic psychology (a small-time crook fantasizing about redeveloping a whole city block) through voice alone (.860/.041). Contrast with R13, card_high/dense_low (.942/.147), whose opening line functions purely as plot-mechanical setup for a crossover reveal, not character revelation.

proposals.name: Reaches real closure rather than an excerpt hook
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the piece reaches an actual ending -- a beginning, complication, and resolution (even a dark or ambiguous one) contained within the text -- versus functioning as an opening or excerpt of a longer work, ending on a hook, a cliffhanger mid-reveal, or a scene-setting line that promises a story not yet begun. High: something has changed and settled by the final line. Low: the final line exists to launch a story the text doesn't actually contain.
proposals.rationale: R32 reaches a complete, self-contained shock ending within a few short paragraphs (dense_high/card_low .943/.030). Contrast with R40, card_high/dense_low (.815/.050), whose story ends on 'Just got back from vacation' -- a line setting up a detective case the text hasn't started (its footer's crossed-out word count also flags it as a truncated/serialized excerpt) -- and R09, also card_high/dense_low (.897/.054), which ends mid-cliffhanger on the villain's taunt with no resolution at all.

proposals.name: Characters individuated by specifics, not trope shorthand
proposals.instruction: Judge whether characters are given specific, non-generic markers of voice or interiority, versus relying on genre-typed shorthand (a funny accent, a stock outlaw nickname, a franchise character imported wholesale) to signal personality without individuating substance. High: the character's specific details (an object, a habit, a turn of phrase) could not be swapped onto a different character in the same genre without loss. Low: the character is legible only as a type -- 'the sadistic interrogator,' 'the tough outlaw' -- via markers common to a whole genre category.
proposals.rationale: R23 gives its dragon-and-rider pair specific, unrepeatable texture (the dragon's razor scales, the boy's self-deprecating 'Grayson Shmayson'); R26 individuates through a precisely observed bonding ritual passed down through 'sixteen generations.' Both dense_high/card_low (.899/.108 and .947/.093). Contrast with R08's Stasi interrogator, characterized entirely through a phonetic 'v for w' accent stereotype, and R18's outlaw 'Smiling Sam,' introduced by nickname-and-type rather than specific detail -- both card_high/dense_low (.865/.093 and .847/.062).

proposals.name: Self-contained fiction that this prompt is load-bearing for
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4. Ask two things: (a) is this text fiction at all, and (b) does the prompt's specific situation generate what happens in it, readable by someone with no outside knowledge. 4 = the prompt's particular constraint drives the central events, and every person, place and reference the reader needs is established inside the text. 2 = a story loosely occasioned by the prompt whose specific constraint could be swapped for a neighbouring one with almost no rewriting, or one that leans on named prior installments the reader has not read. 0 = the text is not fiction (an announcement, a notice, an apology, a note about a story rather than a story), OR the prompt's element appears only as incidental furniture while the actual content belongs to some other ongoing project, OR the text only states the premise and never builds anything on it. Do not reward or punish polish, length, or the presence of an author's sign-off; judge the body of the text.
proposals.rationale: This is the single clearest thing the scorecard appears to over-credit: R36 is an automated moderator removal notice containing no fiction whatsoever, yet it is clean, complete, purposeful, correctly punctuated prose with a beginning, middle and end. R09 hangs six hyperlinks to the author's previous installments on a prompt whose sandwich is pure set-dressing, and introduces Turbo, Emily, Dara, Roger and the Calaveras without establishing any of them. R20 is four lines that state a joke premise and build nothing. All three sit near the top of the scorecard, which suggests the bank scores well-formedness and closure with no gate for whether a story about this prompt exists at all.

proposals.name: Premise enacted through events, never announced as information
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on how the prompt's central conceit reaches the reader. 4 = the conceit is never named outright and is nonetheless unmistakable, carried entirely by what characters do, notice, assume, or conspicuously fail to understand. 3 = named once, late, after being dramatized. 1 = the narrator states the conceit as background early and the story illustrates it. 0 = a character delivers the conceit aloud as information, or the story stops to explain its own mechanism, or a bystander supplies the premise in a line of dialogue. Failing this is not the same as being unclear: a story can score 4 and still be perfectly legible.
proposals.rationale: R13 never once mentions seeing through walls; the power exists only as the student's inability to understand why anyone would need to open the box, and the professor's patient answer is the joke. R30 never uses the words dog, human, cat, or farmhouse, and the whole story is the reader translating. Against these, R40 finally delivers the prompt as a whispered line from a third party (I told you he hates horses, not that he's scared of them), and R07 has the possessed chef announce the twist in explanatory form (I took over your friend, and you thought you defeated me) - both scorecard-high. The bank looks like it credits premise coverage without asking how the premise was delivered.

proposals.name: Withholds something the reader can actually recover
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = there is at least one substantial fact, identity, or relation the story never states outright, the text plants enough for an attentive reader to reconstruct it, and reconstructing it changes how earlier passages read. 2 = mild or local withholding with small consequence. 0 = nothing is withheld - every turn is explained at the moment it occurs and the last line paraphrases the point. Also score 0 if something is withheld but no means of recovery is given, i.e. mystification rather than inference. Judge the recoverability, not the difficulty.
proposals.rationale: R24 never says what the narrator is; the reader assembles it from the switched monitor, the hooked dagger cleaned under the nails, the blood licked off the point, and the resumed cookie. R19 never claims the extent of the narrator's power; the runaway final paragraph of leases, bus stops and tiki bars is the claim. R37 never lists the prompt's three questions - they arrive as 'interbred with, or eliminated'. Contrast R22, where the punchline is stated and then restated by the characters, and R25, whose ending explains itself. All three withholders are dense-high and scorecard-bottom, which suggests the bank rewards stories that say what they mean.

proposals.name: Prose behaviour enacts the condition being narrated
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on whether sentence length, repetition, punctuation, tense or layout perform the state the story is about. 4 = the writing's own habits would have to change if the subject changed, and a reader could infer something of the condition from the shape of the text with the content masked. 2 = one or two local effects. 0 = default paragraph prose applied uniformly regardless of subject. Do not reward mere unusual formatting: the effect must correspond to something in the story. Deliberate roughness that performs a state scores above smoothness that performs nothing.
proposals.rationale: R16 renders anhedonia in flat clipped lines with trailing ellipses and abandoned thoughts - the prose is as low-energy as the infected it describes. R21 counts, loses count, restarts and self-corrects across a three-day loop. R01 writes an incomprehensible beloved in syntax that keeps retracting its own prepositions (close to me, or far away from me, or all of it, at once). All are dense-high and scorecard-low, and each would look like a mechanical defect to a criterion measuring sentence variety or paragraph integrity in the abstract - which is likely exactly what happened.

proposals.name: Formal or register risk taken and carried to the end
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = the piece works in a mode other than default past-tense narrative prose - verse, transcript, liturgy, mock-scholarly history, catalogue, second person - and sustains that mode without lapsing back into ordinary narration to get its work done. 2 = a departure attempted and abandoned partway, or a costume worn for one paragraph. 0 = straightforward narration throughout. A 0 here is not a fault by itself; it simply earns no credit. Penalize below 2 only when a chosen form is dropped precisely at the moment it becomes inconvenient.
proposals.rationale: R29 is a rhymed comic poem with a deliberately bathetic closing couplet (Dave handed Tom 10 quid) and holds the form for its whole length. R32 sustains an institutional-history register complete with invented dynastic events, a cited peasant poet and a parenthetical scandal, never once dropping into scene. R13 is nothing but bracketed speaker labels. All three are top-decile for the dense model and bottom-decile for the scorecard, which suggests the bank's craft criteria presuppose ordinary narrative prose and score everything else as an absence of scene, description or character.

proposals.name: Detail that does work versus decorative inventory
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on what the concrete particulars accomplish. 4 = the specifics imply expertise, economy, danger or social position that the story never states, and deleting them would cost the reader real knowledge. 2 = accurate detail that establishes setting and no more. 0 = nouns catalogued for texture - brands, furnishings, colours, equipment lists - which could be deleted or substituted without any change to what the reader understands. Test each cluster of detail by asking what the reader now knows that they could not have guessed from the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R04 implies an entire trained practice - feeding the arm through the harness to widen it, gripping the traces, taking her down to a knee, sitting her until she stops struggling - and thereby the sixteen generations of family the story asserts only once. R11 makes the family's survival margin arithmetic rather than adjective: half the crop failed, half of the rest only now ripening, enough to cover seed and equipment repairs and winter food and nothing else. Against these, R02 walks its room item by item - vivid blue carpet, racecar bed, silver macbook, 32 inch flat screen, Apple TV - and none of it tells the reader anything the phrase 'childlike bedroom' would not. R02 is near the scorecard ceiling, R04 and R11 near its floor, so the bank appears to be counting sensory density rather than weighing what the density buys.

proposals.name: Figurative coherence rather than simile churn
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on whether the story's images belong to a single governing conception. 4 = figures recur, extend one another, and accumulate into an idea the story could not state directly. 2 = competent isolated images that do not interfere with each other. 0 = high figurative density in which the vehicles change every sentence, none survives into the next paragraph, and the phrases sound literary without letting the reader see anything more precisely. Score the coherence and payoff of the figures, not their frequency or their prettiness.
proposals.rationale: R01 is extremely figurative and every figure serves one project - simultaneity and incomprehension - so that the closing descent into a black hole, where pressure is total and the crushing never completes, is the only place the story's paradox could physically be held. R15 is figurative at a similar rate to no end: a hole like the sighing of whales, then towering words biting down like teeth, then wounds gouged by the fin-beats of giants, three vehicles in two sentences, none of which returns. R28 applies decoration evenly to every noun (Clorox peacemaker, rage ensnaring in thorny coils, swampy skin, plastic trigger). R15 and R28 are both scorecard-high, which suggests the bank rewards imagery counts, while R01 is scorecard-low despite doing the harder version of the same thing.

proposals.name: No exposition delivered to characters who already know it
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on how world rules, history and stakes reach the reader. 4 = through consequence, friction, or a character genuinely ignorant of what they are being told, so the telling is also a scene. 2 = a short unmotivated recap in an otherwise dramatized story. 0 = two or more characters recite to each other facts they both plainly possess - institutional histories, policies, treaties, house rules, each other's motives - so that the dialogue exists to inform the reader. The failure is not the presence of background; it is background spoken by people who have no reason to speak it.
proposals.rationale: R27 has two whales narrate to each other a policy their own body enacted a century ago, the Treaty of Silence, and each other's positions on it - the entire conflict arrives as recited backstory. R14 has the resident ghosts recite the haunted house's four-generation ownership history and its rules aloud, which is the story's only mechanism of information. Both sit in the scorecard's top decile (R27 at the very top of the slice) and near the dense model's floor, so the bank appears to credit worldbuilding and dialogue presence without asking whether the dialogue is doing dramatic work.

proposals.name: Narrator's self-knowledge costs them the reader's approval
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = the point-of-view character reports something about themselves that is genuinely unflattering - envy of a benefactor, pleasure taken in power over others, complicity, cowardice - and the story does not rescue them from it with a redeeming turn or an excusing circumstance. 2 = a flaw admitted and promptly neutralized. 0 = interiority that is uniformly self-justifying, or whose flaws are of the flattering kind (too caring, too loyal). This is about whether the story is willing to lose the reader's sympathy, not about whether the character is a villain: a villain who is simply enjoyed by the text scores low.
proposals.rationale: R31 dismantles its own narrator without letting him off: he admits he never did anything for anyone, that generosity felt like power over people, that praise got him hooked, and refuses the tidy conclusion. R08 lets its protagonist resent the friend who is keeping him alive and housed, and names the resentment ugly without dissolving it. R33 closes on 'Maybe I didn't deserve to.' All three are dense-high and scorecard-low, while R03 - which has no cost anywhere and ends on restored hope - is scorecard-high. A bank measuring character depth or emotional arc would likely score the reassuring one higher.

proposals.name: Ending reframes what preceded rather than announcing closure
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on the final beat. 4 = the last lines send the reader back through the story with changed understanding, using material planted earlier, and the reframing is not stated as a conclusion. 2 = a clean, correct resolution that adds no new reading. 0 = the ending states the moral, the emotion, or the lesson learned, OR introduces a frame in the last line that nothing earlier prepared. Both failures should be scored 0: the announced ending and the arbitrary rug-pull are the same defect, an ending that does not arise from the body of the story.
proposals.rationale: R04 plants a secret fear in one withheld sentence and pays it off in four final words - 'I would have to fly' - which recolours the whole hatching, including the narrator's suppressed hope that the egg had died. R37 answers all three of the prompt's questions at once in a subordinate clause about interbreeding with or eliminating near-peer species. Against these, R25 arrives at 'I've gotta stop gambling' with nothing behind it, and R03 closes by telling us hope was not over after all. The two announced or arbitrary endings are scorecard-high; the two reframing endings are scorecard-bottom, which suggests the bank credits the presence of a twist or a resolution rather than its preparation.

proposals.name: Something is not restored; the piece declines reassurance
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on whether the ending leaves a cost standing. 4 = a loss holds, a pressure remains, or the sympathetic reading has been complicated by the end, and that cost was prepared by the story. 2 = a mostly restored situation with a residue of unease. 0 = the threat is expelled, the curse is lifted, the shift ends, and the closing image returns everyone to comfort. Important: do not reward bleakness pasted on. A grim ending with no preparation scores no higher than a warm one; what is scored is whether the story was willing to let its own events matter.
proposals.rationale: R30 lets the alpha die with no rescue and no consolation beyond the narrator's decision to keep working, and the refrain that opened the story returns with its meaning changed. R33's subject is shot dead in paragraph two and the narrator's response is to stop telling stories at all. Against these, R28 expels the demon with a bleach bottle and ends with the sisters warm under a blanket, R05 books a service appointment and magics the clock to quitting time, and R17 cures the curse and walks the friends home joking. The three restorative pieces are all scorecard-high and R28 is at the very bottom of the dense model's range for this slice, so the bank may be rewarding satisfying resolution as such.

proposals.name: Interest built by the story, not borrowed from known material
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4. 4 = characters, world, and jokes generate their own specificity; where the piece uses a familiar genre or pre-existing characters (which some prompts explicitly require), it supplies a pressure, perception or consequence those sources do not already supply. 2 = competent use of a known register with one original element. 0 = the piece runs on recognition - stock components assembled in the expected order, or imported characters whose entire charge is pre-existing and whose meeting merely confirms what a reader already knows about each. Do not penalize a crossover or a genre exercise for being one; penalize it for adding nothing.
proposals.rationale: R23 flags its own cliche in passing - the narrator finds the single dangling lightbulb a bit cliche - and then plays every other one straight: the phonetically accented interrogator, the defiant wisecracks, the femme fatale rescue with a pistol from the blouse. R06 assembles the noir kit in sequence: tacky Hawaiian shirt, devoted secretary, the ex-wife, the young dame in trouble with a gangster's necklace, the baby blues just like Cece. R38 lets Chigurh and Joffrey carry the whole load; the encounter ends where a reader's prior knowledge of both would predict. All three are scorecard-high. Against them, R19 takes the same prompt-genre and invents a supervillain whose actual power is municipal planning, and lands near the scorecard's floor.

proposals.name: Feeling produced by situation, not named by the narration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4, weighting the story's most emotional moments most heavily. 4 = at the peaks the text stays on behaviour, object, gesture and physical fact, and the emotion word is never supplied - the reader supplies it. 2 = emotions largely dramatized with occasional labelling. 0 = the narration names the feeling at exactly the point it should be enacted, especially in elevated or explanatory formulations that tell the reader how to receive a moment. Score the peaks, not the connective tissue; a story may state feeling in transitions and still score 4.
proposals.rationale: R04 conveys dread and a shameful flicker of relief without a single emotion word: 'I pressed my lips together to keep from smiling. A dead dragon meant a new egg next season.' R30 delivers a death entirely through temperature and stillness - the only heat was my own, and the paw had ceased moving. Against these, R38 supplies 'with the inexpressible sorrow of one who has just learned that he is alone in the universe' at its climax, R07 opens with a captain 'praying to the gods for patience', and R03 closes with 'there'd have to be the biggest smile on my face'. The three labelling stories are scorecard-high and the two staging ones scorecard-low, which suggests the bank may credit emotional content that is legible on the surface.

proposals.name: Living idiolect outweighs surface polish
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on the presence of a specific speaking person. 4 = diction, rhythm, comic timing and habits of attention are particular enough that a paragraph would be recognizable out of context and could not be swapped with another story in the same genre. 2 = a serviceable register with occasional individuality. 0 = clean, correct, interchangeable narration of the kind any competent writer would produce for this prompt. Binding rule for this criterion: do NOT raise the score for correct spelling, grammar or punctuation, and do NOT lower it for typos, comma splices, malapropisms or non-native constructions. Score only how distinct and how consistently held the voice is.
proposals.rationale: R12 misspells throughout (Fist Aid Kit, Grayson Shmayson, the wishing of his mighty tail) and is nonetheless unmistakably one nervous, self-deprecating, fond cadet from first line to last. R35 holds a flat conversational register whose casualness about five killings is the entire effect, typos and all. R37 is error-strewn and still has an identifiable deadpan lecturer behind it. All three are dense-high and among the lowest scorecard rows in the slice (R37 is the lowest). Meanwhile R07 and R38 are mechanically cleaner and voiced by nobody in particular, and both are scorecard-high - the pattern one would expect if the bank contains grammar, clarity and readability criteria and no criterion for whether anyone is speaking.

proposals.name: Comic premise escalates instead of repeating at one pitch
proposals.instruction: Score 0-4 on any piece with a comic or absurd premise (score N/A and skip only if the story is wholly non-comic). 4 = the joke's terms are raised, complicated, redirected or turned against themselves as the piece proceeds, so that the last instance is materially different from the first and the reader could not have predicted the final position from the opening one. 2 = a joke developed once. 0 = one gag or one register sustained at constant amplitude for the whole length, or a single joke delivered and then explained by its own characters.
proposals.rationale: R19 escalates from a small joke about running out of improvised monologue, to a hostage situation being run as professional development for the hero, to a closing paragraph revealing the narrator has been quietly rearranging every business in town for the public good - each step recontextualizes the last. R18 repeats dismemberment at rising absurdity while the victim curses the author by name, so the running gag and the prompt's fourth-wall requirement are the same device. Against these, R39 holds surfer dialect at one level for its whole length with the ending arriving from outside the joke, and R22 states a platypus gag and then has its own characters restate it. R39 and R22 are scorecard-high, R19 and R18 near its floor, which suggests the bank may credit humour presence or consistency of comic voice rather than comic development.

proposals.name: Premise Drives Consequences
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual premise directly causes the characters’ choices, conflicts, and ending; score low when it is merely decorative or supplies a final joke.
proposals.rationale: R01, R10, and R25 make the speculative premise govern the whole emotional situation, unlike the more incidental premise use in R05 and R12.

proposals.name: Revealing Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when concrete sensory details, habits, objects, or gestures simultaneously reveal character, setting, and emotional state; score low when description is generic, ornamental, or interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: The taxi imagery in R01, the physical dragon handling in R26, and the rituals in R34 carry several kinds of information at once.

proposals.name: Earned Emotional Turn
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s emotional stance changes because of specific events and the change is shown through behavior or language; score low when emotion remains static or is simply announced.
proposals.rationale: R01, R21, and R34 convert their premises into discernible changes in resignation, agency, or grief rather than merely naming a mood.

proposals.name: Contradictory Characterization
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s self-image, motives, and behavior conflict in a revealing way; score low when characters remain one-note embodiments of a trope or attitude.
proposals.rationale: R11, R23, and R28 give their protagonists morally uncomfortable motives beneath their outward roles, creating tension the surface plot does not state directly.

proposals.name: Causal Scene Progression
proposals.instruction: Score high when each major beat changes the stakes, information, or available choices and later events follow from earlier ones; score low when the story is a sequence of loosely connected incidents or exchanges.
proposals.rationale: The confrontations in R14, R18, and R26 escalate through decisions and consequences, whereas several scorecard-favored sketches mainly accumulate premise-related events.

proposals.name: Payoff-Ready Foreshadowing
proposals.instruction: Score high when earlier details prepare a later reveal or reversal and acquire fuller meaning afterward; score low when the ending depends on an unprepared twist or simply restates the setup.
proposals.rationale: R01’s repeated lateness, R14’s fatherly reassurance, and R18’s seemingly harmless guard behavior all become more significant after their later turns.

proposals.name: Implicit Worldbuilding
proposals.instruction: Score high when institutions, customs, history, and rules emerge through behavior, objects, and constraints rather than explanatory summary; score low when the story supplies lore without dramatizing its consequences.
proposals.rationale: R08 and R13 reveal entire social systems through their customs and institutional reactions, while R03 often explains its mythology directly instead of embodying it.

proposals.name: Motif That Evolves
proposals.instruction: Score high when a recurring phrase, image, object, or action returns with altered meaning and develops the story’s central concern; score low when repetition is merely emphatic or decorative.
proposals.rationale: The repeated lateness in R01, service refrain in R34, and paradoxical spatial imagery in R25 deepen as their stories proceed.

proposals.name: Voice With Control
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, syntax, figurative language, and narrative distance consistently express a distinctive consciousness while serving the scene; score low when voice is generic or consists mainly of a repeated mannerism.
proposals.rationale: R25’s unstable cosmic language and R34’s formal collective voice are inseparable from their narrators, unlike the largely mannerism-driven dialect in R06.

proposals.name: Tonal Integration
proposals.instruction: Score high when comedy, horror, sentiment, or satire reinforce the same character stakes and remain consequential together; score low when tonal shifts feel pasted on or jokes erase the story’s emotional reality.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R28 use humor alongside violence and compassion without nullifying either, while R24 and R30 frequently substitute gag or spectacle for sustained stakes.

proposals.name: Dialogue With Subtext
proposals.instruction: Score high when speakers pursue different immediate aims, avoid stating the central issue directly, and reveal relationships through wording and interruption; score low when dialogue only explains the premise or trades interchangeable quips.
proposals.rationale: The exchanges in R18 and R28 conceal power and care beneath casual language, whereas R03’s conversations mainly deliver rules and backstory.

proposals.name: Moral Complication
proposals.instruction: Score high when important actions are both understandable and costly from competing moral perspectives, without the narration reducing them to simple labels; score low when heroes and villains are ethically uncomplicated or the story merely states its thesis.
proposals.rationale: R13, R19, and R23 complicate empathy, exploitation, and altruism by exposing uncomfortable motives rather than offering a single moral position.

proposals.name: Non-Obvious Consequence
proposals.instruction: Score high when the premise leads to a surprising consequence or choice that is nevertheless psychologically and causally credible; score low when the story merely lists familiar trope ingredients or performs a shallow inversion.
proposals.rationale: R10 turns universal infection into emotional extinction, R16 turns legal victory into enforced silence, and R27 finds a conceptual consequence inside the classroom joke.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Completeness
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story establishes its own necessary context, relationships, stakes, and resolution; score low when understanding depends on prior installments, external links, licensed familiarity, or an undeveloped fragment.
proposals.rationale: R33 and R35 openly depend on continuing series context, while R29 and R40 provide abbreviated crossover or meta premises without a fully developed independent narrative.

proposals.name: Information Economy
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every sentence advances character, conflict, image, or idea and repetition has a deliberate function; score low when exposition, throat-clearing, or decorative digression can be removed without meaningful loss.
proposals.rationale: R21 and R31 achieve substantial effect through concentrated language, whereas R03 and R32 spend much of their space explaining or ornamenting material that does not change the situation.

proposals.name: Premise as a Causal Engine
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s unusual premise directly causes characters’ choices, conflicts, and events; score low when it merely decorates an otherwise generic scene.
proposals.rationale: R07 makes universal infection drive social and biological consequences, while R09 mainly explains whale institutions around a loosely developing conflict.

proposals.name: Worldview-Specific Perception
proposals.instruction: Score high when narration consistently filters reality through a distinctive character or species worldview; score low when any narrator could describe the same events without change.
proposals.rationale: R01’s dog narrator interprets death and service through animal loyalties, and R14 renders love through cosmic, nonhuman perception.

proposals.name: Concrete Stakes for Abstract Ideas
proposals.instruction: Score high when speculative or philosophical ideas produce tangible bodily, social, or relational costs; score low when they remain generalized explanation.
proposals.rationale: R07 turns emotional numbness into declining pregnancies, while R02 discusses human empathy largely as abstract galactic sociology.

proposals.name: Self-Implication in Character Desire
proposals.instruction: Score high when a protagonist’s goal exposes their own contradiction, weakness, or complicity; score low when characters simply pursue an externally stated objective.
proposals.rationale: R24 makes Mason’s dependence and jealousy part of the central problem, and R40 openly examines the ego behind supposedly charitable behavior.

proposals.name: Moral Ambivalence Without Sermoning
proposals.instruction: Score high when competing values remain genuinely understandable and unresolved; score low when the story announces a simple moral judgment instead of dramatizing one.
proposals.rationale: R31 makes a villain’s schemes simultaneously protective and coercive, while R22 resolves its moral conflict mainly through a declared act of forgiveness.

proposals.name: Subtextual, Differentiated Dialogue
proposals.instruction: Score high when each speaker has a distinct voice and concealed objective, with dialogue changing the relationship or conflict; score low when dialogue only delivers jokes, exposition, or interchangeable reactions.
proposals.rationale: R16 embeds workplace ritual and magical diagnosis in the customer exchange, whereas R10 and R11 rely heavily on overt banter and explanatory lines.

proposals.name: Embodied Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score high when imagined settings and emotions are made credible through precise sensory, physical, and behavioral details; score low when scenes rely mainly on labels such as beautiful, terrifying, or powerful.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses smell, heat, touch, and ritual to ground an animal’s grief, and R18 makes dragon infancy tangible through chewing, wounds, and damaged equipment.

proposals.name: Controlled Repetition and Rhythm
proposals.instruction: Score high when repeated words, structures, or images accumulate changing meaning and regulate pace; score low when repetition is accidental, ornamental, or merely redundant.
proposals.rationale: R01’s recurring service refrain changes from doctrine to mourning, and R32’s counting pattern formally enacts the narrator’s temporal disorientation.

proposals.name: Escalation Through Consequence
proposals.instruction: Score high when each development narrows options or creates a harder subsequent problem; score low when events accumulate without materially changing what characters can do.
proposals.rationale: R34 moves from routine security work to a concealed massacre, while R06 reaches possession quickly but stops before developing its consequences.

proposals.name: Ending Recontextualization
proposals.instruction: Score high when the final image, revelation, or line makes earlier material newly meaningful; score low when the ending merely stops, summarizes, or supplies an expected punchline.
proposals.rationale: R03’s demon encounter becomes a story about inherited childhood fear and sibling protection, while R27’s ending adds irony but barely develops the preceding courtroom setup.

proposals.name: Compression With Narrative Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when a short or highly selective story efficiently establishes context, character, movement, and payoff; score low when brevity produces a sketch or when length adds little usable information.
proposals.rationale: R26 compresses an alien-homecoming reversal into a compact poem, whereas R29 compresses its premise into a single gag without meaningful development.

proposals.name: Relationship as Story Engine
proposals.instruction: Score high when a relationship produces decisions, reversals, or mutual change rather than merely supplying background; score low when characters remain functionally isolated despite interacting.
proposals.rationale: R18’s cadet-dragon bond drives the protagonist’s identity and resolve, while R17’s companions mostly exchange jokes without changing one another’s situation.

proposals.name: Thematic Resonance Beyond the Gimmick
proposals.instruction: Score high when the speculative device illuminates a broader human concern through the story’s particulars; score low when the premise exists mainly for novelty or a one-step joke.
proposals.rationale: R36 turns superpower distribution into a study of guilt, responsibility, and intervention, while R10 uses divine budgeting chiefly to explain a comic animal design.

proposals.name: Coherent Original Recombination
proposals.instruction: Score high when familiar genres, tropes, or source elements are combined into a unified and surprising dramatic logic; score low when references remain recognizable pieces without a new synthesis.
proposals.rationale: R14 fuses cosmic horror with reciprocal romance into one governing metaphor, and R30 transforms courtship conventions into a coherent satirical economic system.

proposals.name: Follow-Through and Closure
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story develops its central problem to a satisfying state of consequence, decision, or understanding; score low when it ends at the setup, an arbitrary interruption, or an unresolved excerpt.
proposals.rationale: R01 carries the alpha’s death through grief into continued duty, while R02 and R06 end just as their central external threats are about to become consequential.
